about.title: About Me
about.p1: I’m Vladi Georgiev, a developer from Bulgaria based in Eindhoven. After studying electronic trades in high school I earned seven professional front-end certificates from Meta, and I haven’t stopped since: over the past year I’ve gone from simple front-ends to shipping full-stack, cross-platform apps.
about.p2: These days I work with React, Next.js and TypeScript on the web, Expo and React Native on mobile, and C# and Node with PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL on the back end. I design everything in Figma, tinker with C++ for hardware, and in DevMatch I connected the app to external APIs and MCP-driven AI agents.

devmatch.title: DevMatch
devmatch.desc: A full-stack, AI-powered job assistant for developers. An Expo React Native app backed by a Node and Express API finds jobs, scores your resume against each listing with ATS analysis, and helps you apply with tailored cover letters.
devmatch.outcome1: Cross-platform Expo app + typed Node/Prisma backend
devmatch.outcome2: AI ATS flow that scores and rewrites resumes per job
devmatch.outcome3: JWT auth, job matching, resume upload and tracking

log.title: Four windows per application
log.body: Applying as a developer meant a job board, a resume, a cover letter draft and a tracking sheet open side by side. I wanted one app that reads the resume once and reuses it for every job.

log.title: No scraping
log.body: LinkedIn and Indeed forbid scraping, so the feed comes from two official APIs: Adzuna for country-specific roles, Remotive for remote ones. Page one mixes them three to one, and each query is cached for 15 minutes so the free tier survives a demo.

log.title: A score before the AI answers
log.body: Asking Gemini about every card would take seconds and burn the quota. Cards first show an on-device estimate (60% tag overlap, 40% title keywords); then one Gemini call scores up to 25 jobs and swaps the numbers in, usually 3 to 5 seconds later.

log.title: Small model, strict JSON
log.body: Flash-Lite answers in 2 to 4 seconds and was free while prototyping. Every prompt asks for raw JSON and shows the schema. It still wraps replies in code fences now and then, so the backend strips those before parsing.

log.title: Practice, not just paperwork
log.body: The interview coach reads the resume and asks five questions: two behavioural, two technical, one situational. Each answer is graded on Situation, Task, Action and Result, then rewritten the way it should have sounded.

snags.problem: Gemini returned 503 when two AI features fired back to back.
snags.fix: Retries with back-off at 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, and an error that tells “overloaded” apart from “quota gone for today”.

snags.problem: Resumes exported from Canva came out of the PDF parser as garbage.
snags.fix: Pasting the resume as text became a first-class option next to upload, not a hidden fallback.

snags.problem: Google and LinkedIn sign-in rejected Expo Go’s exp:// redirect.
snags.fix: Shipped email and password with JWT, and parked social login for a proper development build.

snags.problem: Expo Router only passes strings between screens.
snags.fix: A small module-level store hands the full job object to the detail screen.

ourgrid.title: OurGrid (Client OpenRemote)
ourgrid.desc: A platform demystifying 'grid congestion' for the company OpenRemote. I designed the UI and validated the UX with real users (students & coaches) to translate complex data into a clean React interface.
ourgrid.outcome1: Validated UX via testing with real users
ourgrid.outcome2: Architected a split-view UI for Residents vs. Municipalities
ourgrid.outcome3: Translated technical IoT data into accessible web components

log.title: A headline problem nobody can picture
log.body: Grid congestion keeps making Dutch headlines, yet it stays abstract for the households who cause the evening peak. OpenRemote asked for two things: explain it, and give residents a reason to shift their usage.

log.title: Two front doors
log.body: The first screen asks one question: are you a resident, or do you work with the municipality? The answer lives in a React context and decides which dashboard, charts and wording you get from there on.

log.title: Show the peak, ask for one thing
log.body: The resident view plots the transformer load through the day and marks the risky window, with a single request: avoid heavy appliances between 16:00 and 18:00. One time window instead of a page of tips.

log.title: Nobody’s house on the map
log.body: Municipalities see hotspots, load per neighbourhood and participation, but always aggregated at transformer level. No chart can point at a single household.

log.title: Front end, end to end
log.body: I led the React client: both onboarding paths, the two dashboards, the charts and the explainer pages, and tested the flows with students and coaches. My commits are the largest share of the repo.

figure.title: The peak, before and after
figure.caption: Transformer load from the prototype’s demo data. The “after” line is illustrative: same energy, moved out of the peak.

snags.problem: No live grid feed was available while we built the interface.
snags.fix: A small Express endpoint serves demo data, so every chart was built against a real API shape instead of hard-coded numbers.

snags.problem: A realistic congestion map could imply real households.
snags.fix: Hotspots are drawn per neighbourhood and the map says “illustrative, not real data” in the image itself.

snags.problem: Residents and officials need different words for the same numbers.
snags.fix: One audience choice at the start switches the routes and copy, while the data stays the same.

visiobal.title: Visiobal (Client Visio)
visiobal.desc: An interactive audio ball that lets visually impaired people find, connect to and play with it through sound. A 3D-printed sphere houses an ESP32 that synthesises music on-device and pairs with a companion app over Bluetooth LE: scan to connect, set the volume, and switch between tracks.
visiobal.outcome1: Built and designed the companion app for the ball
visiobal.outcome2: Made the ball fully controllable from the app over Bluetooth LE
visiobal.outcome3: Accessible-by-design play for visually impaired users

log.title: A ball you find by ear
log.body: Visio supports children who are blind or visually impaired. An ordinary ball is useless once you can’t tell where it rolled, so ours plays music the whole time it’s switched on.

log.title: Connect once, stay connected
log.body: The app scans for the device called VisioBal, shows a radar while it searches, and keeps one Bluetooth session alive across every screen instead of reconnecting per page.

log.title: Commands are plain words
log.body: The app writes short strings to a single Bluetooth characteristic: SONG1 to SONG5 pick a tune, SLEEP and WAKE handle power. The ball checks the value and switches tunes on its next control tick.

log.title: No audio files on board
log.body: Every tune is a list of note frequencies and durations. The ESP32 synthesises it live: a triangle-wave lead, a quieter square-wave harmony, an envelope per note, out to the speaker over I²S. I worked on this part together with my teammate.

log.title: The app I built
log.body: Expo and TypeScript: a 3D model of the ball you can spin, a player with volume and a frequency slider, light and dark themes, and English, Dutch, French, German and Bulgarian.

figure.title: From a tap to a tune
figure.caption: The signal chain, then the ball’s five real songs, played in your browser from the same note lists and wave shapes the firmware uses.

snags.problem: Going to sleep straight from the Bluetooth write callback.
snags.fix: The callback only releases a semaphore. A FreeRTOS task sends SLEEPING, waits 500 ms for it to leave, then enters light sleep; any Bluetooth packet wakes the ball.

snags.problem: GCC 14.2 linked a nearly empty libstdc++ stub and C++ symbols went missing.
snags.fix: A post-build script copies the full library over the stub before linking.
Anything that talks to the ball runs in a development build via expo run:android.

snags.problem: Raw knob readings made the volume and pitch jitter.
snags.fix: Both pass through smoothing filters (0.95 for volume, 0.85 for pitch) before they reach the oscillators.
